title: Heat stress gave no clear link to the presence of bleaching percentages in four Atlantic and Pacific samples in 2003-2019
abstract: We tested whether surface heat stress was linked to the presence of a coral bleaching percentage in archived Reef Check surveys. Four site, year, and month models used 7,103 repeated-site records in the Atlantic and Pacific in 2003-2010 and 2011-2019. Slopes ranged from -1.108 to +1.106 reporting percentage points per four TSA degree-heating weeks. All four adjusted working intervals included zero. Five sensitivity designs did not establish a common link. The later Atlantic same-month sample had no missing outcomes and could not give an informative test. These results do not establish random reporting or absence of selection bias. Selected surveys, unknown visit and observer records, coarse surface heat, near-complete reporting in one group, and few year clusters limit inference. The package contains source hashes, a record-level reporting panel, code, all results, a figure, and independent checks. This is a test of an archive observation process, not a test of coral mortality, air pollution, or causal climate change.

display.caption: Within-site heat and reporting slopes in four ocean-period samples. Working country-plus-year cluster intervals use a four-test adjustment.
